title: Seventy times seven
hook: Peter asks: seven times? Jesus: seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22)
carry: a number too big to keep track of

segments.voice: Yesterday, trespasses, the hinge in the Lord's Prayer. Your line was a full cup spills. Which small debt did you stop collecting? Today, a disciple asks how many times that has to happen. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

How many times is enough? Ask it about the roommate who leaves the dishes, again, or the coworker who takes credit in the meeting, says sorry after, and does it the next week. The first time, letting it go feels generous. The third time it feels foolish. Somewhere around there, a reasonable person starts asking where the line is. Peter, one of Jesus's closest followers, asked exactly that, out loud, and even offered a number that sounds generous. Today: seventy times seven.
screen: `AGAIN. AND AGAIN.` → `WHERE'S THE LINE?` → `PETER OFFERS A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Matthew tells it in two short verses. In the King James words, Peter asks: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Notice the shape. It isn't a stranger. It's my brother, someone close, someone who will keep showing up. And Peter's number isn't stingy. Seven times is a lot of patience with one person. Second, the answer. Jesus says: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Some readers take the Greek as seventy times seven, others as seventy-seven times. Either way, the point isn't a bigger number to count up to. It's a number too big to keep track of. If you're tallying to seventy-seven, you've missed the point. The answer quietly takes the counting away. Third, a companion line. Luke's Gospel has a version of this teaching that is even more domestic: "if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Seven times in one day. That's not a betrayal once a decade. That's ordinary life, with someone you live alongside. Fourth, what it doesn't say. The answer doesn't tell Peter to pretend nothing happened, or to stop telling his brother the truth. In Matthew, the verses just before this one lay out how to go to a brother who has wronged you and speak to him directly. Some Christian teachers read the two together: you can name the wrong, set a limit, even keep your distance, and still refuse to keep a running total in your heart. Forgiveness, in this reading, is about the count kept inside, not about letting harm continue.
screen: `HOW OFT? TILL SEVEN TIMES?` · `A NUMBER TOO BIG TO COUNT.` · `SEVEN TIMES IN A DAY.` · `NAME IT, BUT STOP THE TALLY.` · then, large: `UNTIL SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Picture one thing someone close to you does again and again. Not something dangerous, just something that wears on you. Notice the little counter in your head: that's the fifth time, the tenth time. For these two minutes, try setting the counter down. You can still think it's wrong. You can still plan to talk about it. Just let the number go. Each time the tally comes back, and it will, breathe out and set it down again. If you pray, you can name that person once more, without a number attached. The bell holds the time.
Peter. The disciple who asked Jesus how often to forgive, and got an answer too big to keep count. Today's word.
Your line: a number too big to keep track of. Today, forgive the same small thing again, the one you're tired of forgiving, and notice whether you're still counting. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Christian teachers turn to Matthew 18:21–22 when speaking about forgiveness in families and congregations, and preachers sometimes pair it with the verses just before it on going to the person who wronged you.

fork.setup: you're Peter. your brother keeps wronging you, and you want to be generous. what number do you offer Jesus?
options: as many as it takes, no limit.
fork.reveal: Peter offers seven, which is already patient. the answer, seventy times seven, makes the counting itself the problem.
